Last Thursday (October 15), Tesla's new Roadster drove off a ramp that curled over until the car was upside down, rolled upright in the air and landed. It then used thrusters to hop over a Cybertruck. Turns out the future does have flying cars.

The demo had already been pushed back two weeks, "due to high winds" ( Elon Musk on X ). That made us wonder: with a language model in the pilot's seat, how would the car do in that wind?

We built an RL environment around a physics simulator of a flying roadster to find out, handed the controls to LLMs, and turned the wind up. We let some of the latest best models fly it: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Meta's Muse Spark Open, Reflection's Beam 1.0, NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, TypeSafe's Jev 1.14, and even OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra.

Asked for decisions in real time, these models crashed almost every flight: most take 1 to 6 s to answer, and the car needs a new action every 0.2 s. When we paused the world so the models could think as long as they wanted, they still lost to a 4B model we trained with RL in a storm.

Storm, 33 m/s wind: DeepSeek, with unlimited time to think, comes down leaning and hits the road with its body. Our RL-trained 4B lands level.

TL;DR

- We built an RL environment around a physics simulator of a flying roadster with four air thrusters, gusty wind and the reveal's two stunts: a ramp flip and a kickflip over a Cybertruck. An LLM flies it with one command every 0.2 s while the car keeps moving.

- The latest open models can't fly it in real time. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Nemotron 3.5 Super, Muse Spark Open and Beam 1.0 take 1 to 6 s per decision and land 0% of kickflips and 3% or less of ramp flips. GPT-6 Astra also lands 0% on the clock.

- RL post-training made a 4B model our best pilot. Qwen3-4B, trained for about $13, answers in 0.09 s and lands 90% of kickflips in real time. With the world paused for the model to think, the best open model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, lands 87% and the other open models land 58 to 62%. Even GPT-6 Astra lands only 74%.

- Everything is open source, and you can fly your own model without a GPU ( Try it ).

Watch how the models fly the car. Pick a stunt, a wind level and a model below to replay the same flight on a held-out scene. The full page also shows the pilot decision every 0.2 seconds, the telemetry the model saw, and how long each reply took.

## RL environment for flying Tesla Roadster in the wind #

### Four air thrusters lift the car, and push it down when it's upside down

The car is a rigid body, 4.5 m long and 2,000 kg dry, simulated at 500 Hz. Lift comes from four cold-gas thrusters at the corners of the floor of the car. Each thruster is good for 12 kN, fed from one tank of compressed air (110 to 170 kg per flight). They push straight out of the floor. If the left pair fires harder, the car rolls, and if the front pair fires harder, it pitches.

When the car is upside down, the same thrusters push it toward the ground, and that is what makes both stunts hard.

### A car falling flat or sideways catches far more wind

A car is built to move nose first. When it falls flat, or the wind hits it from the side, it shows five to nine times as much area to the air, so the wind pushes it around far more. Near the road the wind is weaker, and gusts come on top of the average. Each flight gets a mean wind from a random direction, in one of three bands: light (up to 14 m/s), gale (14 to 24 m/s) or storm (24 to 33 m/s).

### The wheels can take a 4 m drop, but the roof can't touch the ground

### Two stunts from the reveal: a ramp flip and a kickflip over a Cybertruck

In the ramp flip, a ramp curls over and the car leaves the deck upside down 10 to 14 m up, then has to roll upright and land. In the kickflip, the car comes in at 50 to 94 km/h, clears a parked Cybertruck, rolls a full 360 degrees and lands.

A flight succeeds only if the car ends up on all four wheels on the 14 m road, within about 20 degrees of level, no longer spinning, and without a crash. Every task randomizes the speed, the air in the tank, the wind and gusts, and the ramp size or truck position. The held-out tasks use seeds that no model trained on.

The truck part of each line also gives the time until the car reaches the truck and the time until it's past it, at the current speed, so the model doesn't have to do that division itself. Every LLM in this post sees the same lines, and the hand-written pilot below reads the same numbers.

The five commands are coast (all thrusters off), climb (stay level at a given vertical speed), hold (hold a given roll and pitch), rotate (spin about one axis to a total angle, braking to stop on it) and land (level out and come down softly). The model picks one command, with its numbers, in each reply. A flight computer then turns that command into thrust for each of the four thrusters, 50 times a second, until the next reply arrives.

### The car doesn't stop while the model thinks

If a model takes 2 s to answer, the car flies ten 0.2 s intervals on the old command before the new one takes over. We time every reply end to end. Only the first decision is untimed, like a plan made before takeoff.

We picked 0.2 s because the kickflip's roll takes about a second and has to start within a few tenths of a second of the right moment. With one second between decisions, no pilot could time it, whether model or script. To separate judgment from speed, we also fly every model a second way, with the simulator paused until each reply arrives, so the model has unlimited time to think.

### Half the reward is for a clean landing

For RL the reward runs from 0 to 1. It gives partial credit for height, clearing the truck, rotation and touchdown quality, then 0.4 for a successful landing and 0.1 for a clean finish (soft, with air left, centered on the road).

### A pilot written by hand shows that both stunts can be flown

Before training anything, we wanted to know that both stunts can be flown with these five commands. So we wrote a pilot by hand: a few dozen lines of if-then rules that read the same telemetry and send commands through the same 0.2 s interface. On the kickflip, for example, it starts climbing when the truck is 1.1 s away, starts the roll once the car is 1.4 m above the truck's roof, leans against any sideways drift, and lands once the car is past the truck.

The hand-written pilot answers instantly and sees the same inputs to the LLMs. It lands every light-wind ramp flip and 98% of light-wind kickflips, but only 61% of kickflips in a storm. We call it the scripted pilot in the rest of this post.

The scripted pilot flying both stunts in light wind.

## The latest open models can't fly in real time #

We flew four open models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Muse Spark Open, Nemotron 3.5 Super and Beam 1.0), GPT-6 Astra in storms, and Jev 1.14, a model built for fast decisions that picks from a menu of commands instead of writing JSON. Every model flies the same held-out flights as our trained pilot: 192 per stunt in light wind and in a gale, and 384 in a storm. All runs use temperature 0 and each model's default reasoning setting. We called the open models through OpenRouter, with Nemotron, Muse and Beam each pinned to one provider.

### With time to think, the models make good calls

When the simulator waits for each reply, the four open models fly the kickflip well in light wind. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash lands 98%, and Muse, Nemotron and Beam land 72 to 82%.

Wind makes it harder even then. In a storm, DeepSeek drops to 87%, Muse to 62%, Nemotron to 60% and Beam to 58%. GPT-6 Astra lands 74% of storm kickflips.

### On a running clock, they land 0% of kickflips

With the car moving, all four open models land 0% of kickflips. Their median decision takes 1 to 6 s, so a typical command arrives 5 to 29 intervals after it was needed. In the real-time runs, with 16 flights in parallel, replies were slower still (DeepSeek's median was 2 to 3 s).

GPT-6 Astra takes about 2 s per decision and lands none of its 768 storm flights in real time. On the same clock, our trained 4B lands 90% of storm kickflips.

DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on the same flight, twice. On the left the simulator waits for each reply, and the car lands. On the right the clock keeps running, the replies arrive late, and the car crashes.

### Answering faster doesn't fix it

In our first round, with reasoning off, DeepSeek answered in 0.3 s but made worse calls, and Muse and Beam at low effort still took about 2 s per decision. Jev answers in about 0.17 s, fast enough for the clock, but it lands only 2% of storm kickflips live. A pilot has to answer fast and make good calls.

### The ramp is easier, but the replies still come too late

The car leaves the deck upside down 10 to 14 m up, and a simple plan works: roll upright, lean against the wind, then brake and land. With the simulator paused, the big models fly it. Muse lands 88 to 97%, DeepSeek about 80%, and GPT-6 Astra 383 of 384 storm flights.

On the clock, none of them gets past 3%. The first command is usually a roll upright, which is correct, but the fall takes under 2 s, and the next reply comes after the car has already hit the road.

Not all high-speed interconnects are created equal, and using the wrong one can be quite costly: running the same distributed training job over InfiniBand rather than NVLink can degrade performance by 43% .

Historically, NVLink was limited to communication within a single node, meaning that multi-node AI workloads were forced to communicate over InfiniBand or a cloud equivalent (EFA on AWS, GPUDirect-TCPX on GCP). NVIDIA’s NVL72 systems remove this limitation by connecting all 72 GPUs in a rack with a unified NVLink fabric, so GPUs on different nodes can exchange data with an order of magnitude more bandwidth.

However, maximizing the benefits of NVL72 systems is highly dependent on workload placement: a multi-node job spread across racks is still bottlenecked by InfiniBand. Preserving rack-locality gets harder as hardware failures take nodes offline and jobs finishing at different times scatter free capacity across racks.

This blog covers the communication bottleneck in large-scale training and inference, the NVL72 rack-scale fabric, and slice sizing for resilience to GPU failures, as well as how the SkyPilot Platform keeps multi-node jobs rack-local through topology-aware placement, in-place recovery from hardware failures, and automatic defragmentation of shared clusters.

## Training at scale is a communication problem #

Frontier training jobs run across thousands of GPUs. Doing so requires answering two questions:

- How do you shard your model across GPUs to ensure that it can actually run?

- Given your compute budget, how many copies of the sharded model can you run to maximize training throughput?

The first question is typically answered with a combination of:

- Tensor Parallelism (TP): splitting a layer’s weight matrices across GPUs

- Expert Parallelism (EP): placing a mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer’s experts on different GPUs

- Pipeline Parallelism (PP): splitting a model layer-wise across GPUs

The answer to the second question sets the degree of Data Parallelism (DP): the number of copies of the sharded model that train in parallel, each on a different slice of the training data.

Of these parallelism strategies, tensor parallelism’s all-reduce and expert parallelism’s all-to-all communication patterns sit on the critical path during training, making them the most important to keep on NVLink (§9.1.2).

### Tensor Parallelism

Tensor parallelism splits the weight matrices inside each layer across GPUs, so every GPU only stores and computes a slice of each layer.

Transformer layers are made up of two blocks: self-attention and a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). At its core, each block is two matrix multiplications (GEMMs) in a row. Megatron-LM (§3) showed that by partitioning a block’s first GEMM column-wise and its second GEMM row-wise, the GPUs only need to synchronize via all-reduce once per block, after the second GEMM, instead of after each one.

Even with this optimization, tensor parallelism still requires two all-reduces per transformer layer during the forward pass. These all-reduce steps sit on the critical path during training because they cannot be fully overlapped with computation. As a result, tensor parallelism is typically kept on NVLink: Hugging Face measured a 43% drop in training throughput when it moved off NVLink onto InfiniBand.

### Expert Parallelism

In a mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer, the MLP block is replaced by many smaller MLPs, called experts, and a router that sends each token to a small subset of experts. Expert parallelism splits MoE layers such that these small, independent experts are placed on different GPUs.

Under expert parallelism, each MoE layer requires two all-to-all communication steps during the forward pass, dispatch and combine. A router selects the top- k experts for each token and dispatches tokens to the GPUs that have those experts in memory. Each GPU then computes its local experts on the tokens it received via a single grouped matrix multiplication. Finally, the expert outputs are sent back to each token's original GPU and combined.

As models add more MoE layers and route each token to more experts, the volume of all-to-all traffic grows, introducing a communication bottleneck.

Training an MoE model with 64-way expert parallelism spreads each MoE layer’s experts across 64 GPUs. On standard 8-GPU servers, that moves the all-to-all traffic off high-bandwidth NVLink and through much narrower InfiniBand interconnects where unoptimized communication can consume up to 60% of training time (§1.2). On NVL72 systems, all 64 GPUs stay within a single NVLink domain, effectively eliminating the communication bottleneck (§9.2.2).

## Inference needs fast inter-node networking too #

The parallelism techniques discussed above are not unique to training. Beyond enabling inference engines to serve models that are too large for a single GPU, model parallelism can also improve throughput. Splitting a model's weights across more GPUs frees up memory for the KV cache, so the engine can process more concurrent requests or support larger context windows . In some cases, the freed memory grows faster than the number of GPUs: in one vLLM benchmark, splitting a model tensor-parallel across two GPUs increased the amount of KV cache blocks by 13.9x and delivered 3.9x more throughput.

Expert parallelism follows the same logic. With a low degree of expert parallelism, each GPU holds many experts, leaving less room for the KV cache. WideEP, which refers to expert-parallel configurations spanning multiple nodes, significantly reduces the number of experts per GPU. The trade-off is network traffic: every all-to-all now spans more GPUs. On standard 8-GPU servers, an expert-parallel group can span at most eight GPUs before it has to communicate over InfiniBand, where per-GPU bandwidth drops 18x . NVL72 removes this limit by keeping all 72 GPUs in a rack on NVLink. When serving DeepSeek-R1 at interactive speeds, GB200 NVL72 with 32-way expert parallelism delivers up to 4.4x higher throughput per GPU than 8-GPU B200 servers, which are capped at 8-way.

## The rack is the new server #

NVL72 extends NVLink from a single node to the entire rack, so the whole rack acts like a gigantic accelerator with shared memory .

Every GPU on the NVL72 rack has 18 NVLink ports each delivering 100 GB/s of bidirectional bandwidth, which sums up to a total of 1.8 TB/s for each GPU . Each NVLink port on a given GPU maps to one of 18 NVSwitch chips that power the rack's fabric backplane. Because each NVSwitch chip accepts 72 NVLink lines, one from each of the GPUs, the aggregate internal bandwidth within the rack is 130 TB/s.

This network topology ensures that the fabric is fully non-blocking, meaning that any GPU in the rack can transmit data to any other GPU with uniform latency, making it ideal for large-scale distributed AI workloads.

## Sometimes less is more: using less nodes in each rack significantly improves reliability #

With NVL72 systems, it is tempting to allocate entire 18-node racks to workloads to maximize cluster utilization. In practice, teams actually get more usable capacity out of their cluster by leaving a couple of spare nodes in each rack.

GPUs are unreliable. On its gigawatt-scale supercluster, Meta measured a mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of roughly 490 days per 4-GPU node after putting significant engineering effort into improving reliability. NVL72 clusters make the 72-GPU rack the atomic unit of compute, which increases the fault blast radius by 18x compared to the 4-GPU nodes that make up the rack. The MTBI for the rack is given by:

Based on the formula above, a rack would be interrupted roughly every 490 / 18 ≈ 27 days. If jobs are allocated entire 18-node racks, each of those interruptions makes the entire rack unschedulable until the failed node is repaired. On a 128-rack cluster, this means that a rack would become unusable for full-rack jobs roughly every 5 hours.

Reserving two nodes per rack as spares changes this. When a node fails, a spare in the same rack replaces it, so a single node failure no longer takes the entire rack out of commission. The cost is that two nodes per rack sit idle while everything is healthy.

To quantify this trade-off, NVIDIA modeled how different slice sizes affect usable capacity on a 128-rack (2,304-node) cluster as the share of unavailable nodes grows.

At SkyPilot, we manage tens of thousands of our customers’ GPUs, and on production NVL72 clusters we have measured unavailability rates of around 2%. At that rate, NVIDIA’s model shows that 16-node slices provide 27% more usable capacity than 18-node slices (2,037 vs. 1,602 nodes). They also beat 9-node slices by 4%, even though two 9-node slices fill a rack exactly: with 9-node slices, every failure costs half a rack, while with 16-node slices, the first two failures in a rack are fully absorbed. Compared with 8-node slices, 16-node slices give each job twice as many GPUs per NVLink domain while giving up less than 1% of usable capacity until node unavailability exceeds about 3.3%.

Sixteen nodes is also a natural size for distributed AI workloads: 64 GPUs is a power of two, which matches how parallelism groups are typically sized .

## How a modern scheduler keeps jobs on NVLink #

So far, we have covered why the most communication-heavy parallelism techniques belong on NVLink, how NVL72 extends NVLink from a single node to the whole rack, and why 16-node slices with two spare nodes per rack get the most usable capacity out of production clusters. SkyPilot puts this into practice by placing each slice on a single rack, recovering from hardware failures in-place, and keeping whole racks free as jobs come and go.

### Schedulers need to understand the hardware

Choosing the right slice size is only the first step. How do researchers ensure that each slice of a multi-node training run actually lands on a single rack?

Naive schedulers split multi-node jobs across racks, forcing workers to communicate over InfiniBand (400 Gb/s per direction) instead of NVLink (1.8 TB/s bidirectional) :

SkyPilot’s Topology-Aware Scheduler (TAS) ensures that workers are colocated on the same rack:

For multi-rack workloads, TAS splits the job into 16-node (configurable) slices, and places them each on their own rack with two spare nodes. Then, when SkyPilot’s GPU Manager detects GPU failures, SkyPilot Frontier Trainer can hot swap the faulty node with one of the reserved healthy nodes while the remaining nodes continue running without interruption. To quantify the impact of slice-based scheduling, NVIDIA’s GR00T team compared the effect of two different scheduling policies during pre-training of GR00T N1.7, a multimodal foundation model for humanoid robots, on 512 GB300 GPUs across 128 nodes. The first run used a naive scheduler that placed nodes across an arbitrary number of racks. Rack-aware placement raised throughput by 14.4%, cutting each iteration from 1.59 s to 1.39 s.

On a 10,000-GPU cluster, the same speedup saves roughly $16.7K per training hour. That’s about $400K saved for every training day, just by making better scheduling decisions.

### Fragmentation blocks rack-scale jobs

So far we have explored how topology-aware scheduling works in isolation. In practice, large clusters are typically shared: heterogeneous workloads such as pre-training runs, RL rollouts, and batch inference all compete for the same resources. TAS bin packs workloads within the same rack at scheduling time, but jobs finish at different times, leaving free nodes scattered across racks.
